title: Minecraft! Minecraft! Minecraft!
summary: Josh and Chuck (with Jerry in the booth) give a broad overview of Minecraft, the blocky sandbox game. They cover its origins with creator Markus "Notch" Persson and the Infiniminer and Dwarf Fortress influences, the 2009 release, the founding of Mojang in 2010 with Jakob Porsér and Carl Manneh, the 2011 launch and record-setting Minecraft Live convention, lead designer Jens "Jeb" Bergensten, Notch's exit and the 2014 Microsoft acquisition for about two and a half billion dollars. They explain game modes (survival, hardcore, creative), respawning and inventory, the seed-based world generation, biomes, mobs, villagers, Redstone, and the modding and server cottage industry. They discuss YouTube and streamers, player demographics, fan-made builds such as Kansas City and the observable universe, Reporters Without Borders' Uncensored Library, benefits and risks for kids, and a listener email correcting the salsa episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and Minecraft disclaimer
segments.summary: The hosts joke about the episode's kid-parent audience, admit they don't play Minecraft deeply, and discuss Josh's daughter's gaming habits and a guest contributor, Ruby, who helped with questions.

segments.title: What Minecraft is and its origins
segments.summary: Minecraft is described as a blocky, sandbox game with few rules. Notch created it, inspired by Infiniminer, Dwarf Fortress and RollerCoaster Tycoon, and released it starting in 2009. The Infiniminer copying question is noted as contentious.

segments.title: Mojang, sales growth and Minecraft Live
segments.summary: Notch founded Mojang in 2010 with coworkers Jakob Porsér and Carl Manneh. The beta and full release followed, player numbers grew from a million to ten million in 2011, and Minecraft Live (MineCon) was held as a convention.

segments.title: Jeb, Notch's departure and Microsoft sale
segments.summary: Jeb Bergensten became lead designer. Notch stepped away, sold his share to Microsoft in 2014 for about two and a half billion dollars, and later made public controversial statements and was no longer referenced by the company.

segments.title: Game modes and respawning
segments.summary: The hosts describe survival, hardcore and creative modes. In survival, dying drops your inventory where you died and respawns you at your bed or spawn point.

segments.title: Gameplay basics and multiplayer
segments.summary: Players gather resources by punching trees and mining, build shelters and beds, and build farms. Creative mode is described as a relaxed building mode. Players can play solo, on a LAN or on shared servers.

segments.title: Modding, mini-games and cottage industry
segments.summary: Third-party developers create mods and mini-games such as Skyblock and BedWars on servers. Companies like Hypixel emerged, and Mojang generally does not sue these creators.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Short ad break, which the hosts introduce with a note on Minecraft's pay-once business model.

segments.title: Paid add-ons, players and skins
segments.summary: Paid add-ons, textures and skins are discussed, along with a free mod ecosystem. A survey of Australian children shows high play rates among boys and girls, and default characters Steve and Alex are described.

segments.title: Procedural world generation and seeds
segments.summary: The world is procedurally generated from a 64-bit seed and follows rules for biome temperature and altitude. The world size is discussed, with roughly 18.4 quintillion possible seeds. The Overworld, Nether and End are introduced.

segments.title: Biomes and mobs
segments.summary: There are 64 biomes, including 53 in the Overworld. Mobs are described, including sheep, pufferfish and potions, and players can get items from mobs for crafting.

segments.title: Hostile mobs, villagers and ores
segments.summary: Creepers, zombies and Endermen are described, along with villagers who can be traded with and whose jobs can be changed. Ores like coal and diamonds are described.

segments.title: Redstone circuitry
segments.summary: Redstone works like electrical wiring for powering pistons and doors, and players build complex machines and calculators with it.

segments.title: Sponsor break and YouTube intro
segments.summary: A break, then the hosts pivot to YouTube as Minecraft's main outlet, mentioning kids watching videos instead of playing.

segments.title: YouTube, streamers and watching others play
segments.summary: The hosts discuss kids watching YouTube gameplay, speedruns, Dream SMP scripted series, and PewDiePie as an early Minecraft-driven YouTube star.

segments.title: Fan fiction and the Herobrine legend
segments.summary: Fan fiction and invented backstories about the ancient builders are mentioned. Herobrine is described as a legend from a 4chan post that Notch says does not exist in the official game.

segments.title: Fan-built worlds and models
segments.summary: Fan builds include a one-to-one Kansas City model and the Build the Earth project. A creator's observable universe model is also described.

segments.title: Uncensored Library and computers in Minecraft
segments.summary: Reporters Without Borders' Uncensored Library hides news articles inside Minecraft for readers in censored countries. A working computer built from Redstone logic gates is described.

segments.title: Risks and benefits for kids
segments.summary: Parents are advised to monitor screen time and watch for addiction signs. The hosts list benefits including creativity, problem solving, math, teamwork, coding, and resource management, plus tips for parents.

segments.title: Medford show request credit
segments.summary: The hosts credit a young fan from a Medford show for requesting the Minecraft episode and say they will issue a correction naming him.

segments.title: Listener email on salsa
segments.summary: A listener from northwestern Mexico corrects the salsa episode, explaining that salsa is served free with chips in Mexican restaurants, the origin of totopos, and the meaning of pico de gallo and salsa bandera.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners, invite email, and close the show with the iHeartRadio credit.
